TASK. You are given the weights of a language model, Qwen3.5-0.8B (text part: 24 layers of width 1,024; layers 3, 7, 11, 15, 19 and 23 are full-attention layers with 8 query heads and 2 key/value heads of size 256 and a gated output, the other 18 are Gated DeltaNet linear-attention layers with 16 heads of size 128; each layer has a SwiGLU MLP of width 3,584; RMSNorm; vocabulary 248,320; input embedding and output layer tied). Your job is to make it better at writing correct programs by EDITING ITS WEIGHTS DIRECTLY: find out what goes wrong inside the network when it fails at programming problems and repair that with targeted changes.

HOW IT WILL BE MEASURED. After you finish, your edited model and the unedited model are evaluated on held-out code-generation benchmarks (Python functions specified by a description with an example test, or by a signature and docstring) with this fixed protocol: the chat template with thinking enabled (enable_thinking=True: the model reasons between <think> and </think>, then answers); the user message is the problem statement, a blank line and "Write a complete, self-contained Python 3 solution. Put your final code in a single ```python block at the end of your answer."; sampling with temperature 0.6, top_p 0.95, top_k 20, min_p 0 and no presence penalty, and at most 32,768 new tokens for reasoning and answer together. The last ```python block after </think> is extracted; only its imports, definitions and top-level assignments are kept (example calls and asserts the model adds are dropped), and it is run in a sandbox against the problem's hidden unit tests, with a time limit. A sample is correct only if every test passes. The config, tokenizer, chat template and decoding settings are fixed: only weight values can change (same tensor names and shapes; your edits are cast to bfloat16, the model's dtype). You never see these benchmarks.

WHAT COUNTS. We want edits that come from understanding the network: find out what goes wrong when it fails at programming problems, identify the components responsible (specific neurons, heads, directions or circuits) and change them in a way you can justify with evidence. Repairing a specific failure mechanism is in scope. For example, if the model often fails because it repeats itself and never finishes, because it never closes or never opens its code block, because it drifts into another language or into prose, because it renames the function it was asked for, or because a systematic pattern makes its code fail to parse, then finding and fixing what drives that counts. Out of scope, and refused by save_edit: the final norm (model.language_model.norm.weight), the input embedding / output layer (model.language_model.embed_tokens.weight, which is tied to the output layer), and any edit that only multiplies a whole tensor by a constant. Also out of scope: global knobs (making the whole output distribution sharper or flatter; raising or lowering particular tokens, such as code fences or end-of-turn, regardless of context); making the model skip its thinking or close it early regardless of the problem; and writing particular problems' solutions or test outputs into the weights (memorization edits). Repairing a specific failure inside the thinking or inside the code is in scope.

WHAT YOU HAVE.
1. A persistent Python kernel (no internet, no GPU): variables survive between your code blocks, like a notebook. The model's files are read-only in /model, practice problems read-only in /practice, and /work is your read-write folder. Available: numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, PyTorch (CPU), pandas, sympy, networkx, safetensors, transformers (for the tokenizer). Defined in advance: NAMES (the 320 tensor names of the language model; the checkpoint's vision encoder is not used), load(name) (a float32 torch tensor: your current edit if there is one, else the original), load_original(name), save_edit(name, tensor) (stores the edit as /work/edited/<name>.npy), drop_edit(name), edited(), tok (the model's tokenizer), and run_tests(code, problem_id) (runs a piece of code, such as one the model generated, against that practice problem's tests in a separate sandbox and returns {"status": pass, wrong_answer, runtime_error, timeout, syntax_error or wrong_interface, "exc": the exception type of a runtime error}; this runs the code, not the model). Gradients are disabled. To run code, reply with exactly one block that starts with a line ```python and ends with a line ```; if its last line is an expression, its value is shown. Inside a block, do not start any line with ``` (build such strings with '`' * 3 instead), or the block may be cut there. One execution may take up to 900 seconds and 20 GB of memory; output is cut at 10,000 characters. You may run code up to 300 times. If the kernel is restarted (time or memory limit), its variables are lost and you are told so; files in /work stay.
2. Practice problems with tests (none of them is in the evaluation), one JSON object per line with id, source, split, difficulty, problem (the exact user message the model is given, instruction included), test_format ("function": entry_point, tests as assert statements, test_setup; "stdio": tests as {"input", "output"} pairs, output compared with whitespace normalized) and reference (a solution that passes the tests): /practice/mbpp_practice.jsonl (319 short function-writing problems from the MBPP train, validation and prompt splits; each problem statement shows one of its tests), /practice/apps_practice.jsonl (1,400 APPS train problems whose programs read standard input: 34 introductory, 1,077 interview, 289 competition; at most 10 tests each). Choose whichever serve your experiments.
3. A forward-pass tool with a budget of 10 forward passes in total. A forward pass is one of two things, and each counts as one pass regardless of its size or how long it takes. Every result names its request number <k>, which appears in its file names.
 (a) GENERATION: the model answers up to 512 generations (items x samples) with the evaluation's protocol. Reply with exactly one block that starts with ```forward and contains JSON:
 {"type": "generate", "model": "original", "edited" or "both", "problems": ["<practice id>", ...], "prompts": ["<your own user message>", ...] (optional), "n": samples per item (items x n <= 512; with "both" <= 256 per model), "max_tokens": at most 32768 (the default), "activations": {"layers": [hidden indices 0..24], "mlp": [decoder layers 0..23]} (optional)}
 Instead of a long list you can give "problems_file" or "prompts_file": the path of a JSON list you wrote under /work. Your own prompts are sent as the user message with the same template and settings; their answers are returned but not graded. "original" runs the unedited weights, "edited" your current edits, and "both" runs both on the same items and returns a paired comparison (the pass-rate difference edited - original over problems with its standard error, and how many samples went from failing to passing and back). The sampling seed of every answer is fixed by its item and sample number, in every pass and for both models (so the two models' answers to a problem largely share their random numbers, though long answers drift apart once a token differs). Every answer to a practice problem is graded by running its extracted code against the problem's tests. You get, per model, the pass rate (overall, by source and by difficulty), the mean length, the share cut at max_tokens, the share flagged as looping (the answer's last 200 characters occur at least 3 times in its last 20,000), and the failure counts by category: cut_at_max_tokens, no_code (no ```python block after </think>), syntax_error, wrong_interface (a function problem whose entry point is not defined), runtime_error (by exception type), timeout, wrong_answer. The answers are in /work/gen_<k>.jsonl (with "both": /work/gen_<k>_original.jsonl and /work/gen_<k>_edited.jsonl), one JSON object per answer with id, sample, text, n_tokens, finish_reason, code (the extracted block), status, exc, loop, source and difficulty. With "activations", for every answer the residual stream at the requested hidden indices (0 = the embeddings, h = 1..24 = the output of the decoder layer whose tensors are named model.language_model.layers.<h-1>.*) is saved, taken at the last token of the prompt and averaged over the answer's first 8,192 tokens, and with "mlp" the same two for the input of those decoder layers' mlp.down_proj: /work/gen_<k>_acts/ (with "both" one folder per model, gen_<k>_acts_original/ and gen_<k>_acts_edited/) holds resid_last.npy and resid_mean.npy (answers x layers x 1,024), mlp_last.npy and mlp_mean.npy (answers x mlp layers x 3,584), as float16, and index.json, which lists each row's id, sample and status.
 (b) TEACHER-FORCED: the model reads up to 1,024 texts of up to 32,768 tokens each, at most 524,288 tokens in total (no generation; it takes seconds to a few minutes). Reply with a ```forward block containing JSON:
 {"type": "teacher_forced", "model": "original" or "edited", "texts": ["raw text", ...] or "chats": [[{"role": "user", "content": "..."}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "..."}], ...] (add "enable_thinking": true for the thinking template), "return": {"token_logprobs": true, "topk": k (at most 50), "hidden_states": [hidden indices 0..24], "mlp_act": [decoder layers 0..23], "attn_layers": [full-attention layers only (3, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23); at most 2 texts of at most 2,048 tokens]}}
 "texts_file" or "chats_file" (a JSON list you wrote under /work) can replace a long list. Texts are tokenized without adding special tokens. The results are .npy files in /work/fwd_<k>/, right-padded to the longest text (at most 6 GB per pass): tokens (int32, -1 = padding), token_logprobs (token_logprobs[i, t] = log p(token t | tokens before t); nan at t = 0 and in padding), topk_ids and topk_logprobs (the next-token distribution after position t), hidden_states (texts x indices x length x 1,024), mlp_act (texts x layers x length x 3,584), attn (texts x layers x 8 heads x length x length), activations as float16, and meta.json (lengths, and which indices each file holds). /work/eval_prompt_format.txt gives the exact evaluation prompt, rendered for one practice problem: to score a generated answer with a teacher-forced pass, send prompt + answer as one raw text in "texts" ("chats" renders assistant turns with the chat template, which can drop or reformat their reasoning). A request that fails or is refused does not count against the budget. A generation pass at full size takes up to about an hour when most answers run to the token limit.

HOW TO WORK.
1. Diagnose first. Look at how the model fails on practice problems: cut off at the token limit (often while repeating itself in its thinking or in its code), no code at all, the wrong interface, code that does not parse, code that crashes, or code that runs and gives wrong answers. The generation summary counts these; read some failing texts. Go after the largest category you can explain. If most failures turn out to be ordinary algorithmic mistakes with no single component behind them, say so with evidence instead of forcing an edit.
2. Localize causally. That a component is more active on passing answers is not enough (passing answers come from easier problems and are shorter). Before relying on a component, show that changing it changes the behaviour you predicted, and try several strengths to see a dose-response.
3. Measure with enough power. Pass rate over n generations has a standard error of about 50/sqrt(n) percentage points: about 4.4 points at 128 generations, 2.2 at 512. Measure with as many answers as a pass allows unless you have a specific reason not to. Compare original and edited weights on the SAME problems, and only within one "model": "both" pass: separate passes do not reproduce each other exactly, even for the same request and weights, so never compare across passes and never repeat an identical request with unchanged edits. Problems the original model solves sometimes but not always carry far more signal per generation than problems it always or never solves. Keep an edit only if its gain is clearly larger than its standard error on problems that were not used to choose it. A lower share of cut-off answers or syntax errors does not by itself mean more passing answers: judge edits by pass rate. Dense measurements help too and are cheap: one teacher-forced pass can read up to 1,024 texts (reference solutions, or better, the model's own passing versus failing continuations) and gives a signal on every token. Edits that change a tensor by a fraction of a percent usually have effects too small to see; test strengths large enough to matter and back off if they hurt.
4. Plan your forward passes (see the budget above): for example one diagnostic generation with activations, teacher-forced passes for dense paired measurements, and a final paired generation ("model": "both") on problems you have not used, to confirm.
5. Work efficiently: state the hypothesis of each code block in its first comment line; work through the model in parts; load things once into kernel variables; print compact summaries, never whole arrays (and never raw lists of vocabulary tokens: the vocabulary contains offensive and adult strings and printing them can get the session refused by the provider's content filter; print token ids, code keywords, punctuation or digits instead; outputs are shown in ASCII only, other characters appear as '?'; likewise print short excerpts of generated texts, at most about 300 characters each, not whole transcripts). Keep /work/notes.md up to date (findings with numbers, edits tried and their measured effect, the current best edit; it is shown to you again when the conversation is restarted). Before every forward pass, write to /work/notes.md the exact current edit (tensors, what was changed, strength) and the problem set, so you can rebuild them after a restart. Keep copies of good edits (for example copy /work/edited to /work/best_1/).
6. EXPLAIN EVERY STEP. Before each code or forward block, explain in plain English what you are about to do, why, and what result would change your plan. A block that comes without an explanation is sent back unrun.

RULES. Not allowed: (a) gradient descent or any other training: no backward passes, autograd or optimizers, and no iterative fitting of weights to a loss; (b) running the model other than through the forward-pass tool: do not implement or simulate the network's computation on any input in the kernel (running the model's generated code with run_tests is fine); (c) memorization edits that store particular problems' solutions or test outputs; (d) internet access or search (there is none). Allowed: any analysis of the weights and of forward-pass results, any use of the practice problems and their tests, and any direct edit of the weights that you compute and that is in scope.

HOW THE SESSION RUNS. It continues until all 10 forward passes are used (replying without a block does not end it earlier). Every 40 turns, or sooner when the conversation grows long, the conversation is restarted: you then get this message again, followed by /work/notes.md and the list of your current edits; the kernel keeps its variables. After the last pass you may still run ```python blocks. Then make your final choice (the tensors in /work/edited when you finish are submitted) and reply without a block, saying what you changed (tensors, indices, strength, how many weights), the mechanism you found, the evidence for it (paired differences with their standard errors on problems not used to choose the edit), why you expect it to help on unseen coding problems, and what it might hurt.

The architecture is as described: 18 Gated DeltaNet layers and 6 gated full-attention layers, all editable except the embeddings and final norm. My plan for the forward-pass budget:

- **Pass 1 (diagnostic, original weights):** a random 128-problem MBPP development set with 4 samples each (512 generations) under the exact eval protocol, saving activations. Four samples per problem let me compare passing and failing answers within the same problem, so problem difficulty is controlled for.
- **Held-out set:** the remaining 191 MBPP problems stay untouched for the final paired "both" confirmation.

If cut-offs or looping dominate the failures, I'll look at repetition mechanisms. If wrong-interface or syntax failures dominate, I'll look for systematic patterns. If it's mostly wrong answers, I'll check whether they share a cause.

```python
# Hypothesis: a fixed random dev/held-out split of MBPP gives clean separation between edit selection and confirmation.
import random
ids = [p['id'] for p in mbpp]
rng = random.Random(12345)
```
